titre: Bouba and Kiki: A Robust Effect, but Not a Universal One
accroche: A round shape, a pointy shape, two made-up words: a large majority match them the same way. A 2021 study of 25 languages looks for the exceptions.
contenu_vulgarise:
Two drawings: one a cloud-like shape with rounded edges, the other a star with sharp points. Two made-up words: bouba and kiki. In most experiments, a majority of participants give bouba to the round shape and kiki to the pointy one, without being able to say why. People often conclude that the link between a sound and a shape is universal, written into the species. The literature says something more like this: a strong tendency, with its exceptions.

## Words That Are Not the Original Ones

Bouba and kiki are the words that Ramachandran and Hubbard popularized in 2001 (*Journal of Consciousness Studies* 8(12), pp. 3-34). The phenomenon is older: Wolfgang Köhler had shown it with baluba and takete, then, in the 1947 edition of *Gestalt Psychology* (the first dates from 1929), with maluma and takete. Ramachandran and Hubbard propose an explanation by imitation: the abrupt changes of direction in the pointy outline would evoke the sharp inflections of the sound kiki, and that of the tongue against the palate. This is a hypothesis, which the experiment alone does not demonstrate.

## An Effect That Survives Without Writing

A natural suspicion: the effect would come from the letters, the rounded b, the angular k. Yet the Himba of northern Namibia, who have no written language and little contact with the West, show the same matching (Bremner et al., *Cognition*, 2013). The same researchers nevertheless observe differences in other correspondences: the Himba do not link sparkling water to angular shapes, and they tend to match milk chocolate, which is less bitter, with angular shapes, the reverse of the Western pattern. Some of the links between the senses therefore seem to depend on culture.

## Twenty-Five Languages

In 2021, Ćwiek and his colleagues have speakers of 25 languages, from nine families, written in ten writing systems, take an online experiment. They estimate the average proportion of matching responses at 72% (95% credible interval: 56% to 82%). Speakers of languages written in the Latin alphabet show the effect only slightly more often, and the effect is no stronger when the writing gives bouba a rounder shape: the letters do not explain most of it.

A minority of languages nevertheless departs from the trend: Mandarin, Albanian, Turkish, Romanian. Romanian shows the lowest proportion. The authors note that bouba there recalls bubă, a word for a sore, used mostly with small children, and suggest that the idea of a sharp pain may outweigh that of roundness. This is a lead, not a result. They also report a 2017 meta-analysis (Styles and Gawne): 89% matching responses across 13 experiments conducted in six languages, but no effect among speakers of Syuba, in the Nepalese Himalayas, which Styles and Gawne possibly attribute to phonemes absent from that language or to sound sequences not permitted in it.

## What This Shifts

The link between the sound of a word and what it designates is thought to be arbitrary. Bouba and kiki show that it is a little less so than is claimed, for pseudo-words set before two drawings, but not to the point of making a law: the authors conclude that there is a strong general tendency, modulated by language and culture. Why the exceptions fall on these languages rather than others, they leave to future research.

repere.texte: Across 25 languages, nine families, and ten writing systems, the estimated average proportion of responses matching the bouba/kiki effect is 72% (95% credible interval: 56% to 82%).
repere.source: Ćwiek et al., “The bouba/kiki effect is robust across cultures and writing systems,” Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B 377(1841), 20200390, published online November 15, 2021

carte.punch: Bouba round, kiki pointy: 72% across 25 languages, except in Mandarin, Albanian, Turkish, and Romanian.
carte.idee: The bouba/kiki effect is robust: an experiment across 25 languages estimates it at 72% matching responses on average. It is not universal, however: Mandarin, Albanian, Turkish, and Romanian depart from the trend, and in Romanian bouba recalls bubă, the sore.
carte.source_courte: Ćwiek et al., Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B, 2021

pour_aller_plus_loin.titre: The bouba/kiki effect is robust across cultures and writing systems (full text, in English)

quiz.question: What does the 2021 study of 25 languages conclude about the bouba/kiki effect?
choix: That it disappears as soon as a language is written in an alphabet other than Latin
That it comes mostly from the shape of the letters, the b being round and the k angular
That it is absolute: every speaker tested associates bouba with the round shape
That it is a strong general tendency, with exceptions such as Romanian
quiz.explication: The authors estimate the proportion of matching responses at 72% and speak of a robust general tendency, modulated by language: Mandarin, Albanian, Turkish, and Romanian depart from it. Speakers of languages written in the Latin alphabet show it only slightly more often, and the effect is no stronger when the writing makes bouba rounder, so the alphabet and the shape of the letters do not explain most of it.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What do Bremner et al. (2013) observe among the Himba of Namibia, who have no writing?
choix: They match neither shape and sound nor shape and taste, which would confirm the purely cultural origin of the effect
They associate sparkling water with angular shapes, as Westerners do
They match shape and sound like Westerners, but not shape and taste: they link milk chocolate to angular shapes
They match shape and taste like Westerners, but not shape and sound
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The Himba share Westerners' shape-sound matching, but not their shape-taste matching: they link milk chocolate, which is less bitter, to angular shapes, the reverse of the Western pattern.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What explanation do Ramachandran and Hubbard propose for the bouba/kiki effect?
choix: A universal inheritance written into the species, demonstrated by their 2001 experiment
An imitation: the angular outline would evoke the inflections of the sound kiki and the tongue against the palate
A convention learned in childhood from the shape of the letters of the alphabet
A chance effect, with no mechanism proposed by the two authors
quiz_supplementaire.explication: It is a hypothesis of imitation, not demonstrated by the experiment alone: the angles of the pointy outline would recall the inflections of the sound kiki and the movement of the tongue.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What do Ćwiek et al. report about the meta-analysis by Styles and Gawne (2017)?
choix: 100% matching responses in all six languages tested, with no exception
A weaker effect than the one measured in 2021, around 40% matching responses
No effect in any Himalayan language, not just Syuba
89% matching responses across thirteen experiments, with no effect among Syuba speakers
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Styles and Gawne find 89% matching responses across thirteen experiments in six languages, but no effect among speakers of Syuba, in the Nepalese Himalayas.
